content.text:
Ok so, we got issue workflow in `.aiassistant`. 
My manager, Mathieu, on Slack has created a channel with few teammate, and sent this:
Hello @channel :wave::skin-tone-2:
@Gaël Robin recently worked on more advanced AI workflows, agents and skills than what we usually used at WP Media. He has some promising results, including small tickets found and handled mostly with AI, enhanced AI-based code reviews & testing (including e2e manual tests with AI using the browser), etc.
As an exercise, he ran this on a few tickets for WP Rocket, Imagify & BackWPUp plugins. I would like that we evaluate the results so that:

We gain confidence in the work of AI and the whole WP Media engineering team is confident in adopting in more than what we do today
We identify things it did not do well (issues in the code, way of coding we would not want, unclear tickets, unclear PR descriptions, missed cases while testing, unclear test reports, inaccuracies, really anything that is not on par with our standards) so that we try to refine the agentic system and make it better ; or acknowledge its limitations
We demonstrate the productivity gains we can have, especially on tackling "small" tickets that we would otherwise never really do, but also on more complex tasks


As I mentioned, @Gaël Robin has a system that seems to work very well, but we can only be sure once we get an overall consensus, and once it has been challenged. Therefore, I would like:

@Ahmed Saeed Ghannama & @Rémi Perona to review a few on the PR @Gaël Robin will share (from WP Rocket & Imagify), just like you would review an PRs (the code, the desc, testing it, the usual) and share your feedback here. Anything it did well and anything it missed or shouldn't pass our review. So that @Gaël Robin can improve the system.
@Laurent Molina, you shared in DMs that you tried on a given issue and it did not work. What was the issue? So that @Gaël Robin (& you if you have time) can retry (together) and see how we can improve the system.


That's a first step of reviews/challenges to make the system bullet-proof. Then, I very soon want to organize a 1-day workshop for everyone in WP Media engineering team to dedicate a day to this:

Demo of the system and what it can do, how it works
Reviews from the teammates about the work of the AI (PRs, ticket descriptions, PR comments, reports, etc). Same target: gain confidence & point out issues so we can improve
Try it themselves on a few issues.
So that we adopt the system, or at least part of it.
I would like us to move fast on this. If agenda allows, I'll plan the workshop end of next week so let's iterate quickly on the first tasks mentioned above. OK?
Let's make it, we have a good opportunity here :slightly_smiling_face:


(Gael is me). 



So I'm wondering if we could write a slack message casual to explain overall the system, the workflow. the capabilities. 
And we need a list of issue, best way right now is Imagify-plugin, where we did work on some issues: 
We can add a small text for each each explaining what the AI did:
https://github.com/wp-media/imagify-plugin/pull/1054
https://github.com/wp-media/imagify-plugin/pull/1055
https://github.com/wp-media/imagify-plugin/pull/1056
https://github.com/wp-media/imagify-plugin/pull/1058

Let's create a slack.md at the root of the project. 

Also we can add something about our different setup across plugins:
- Imagify is the most complete one as it integrates e2e and CI for e2e.
- WP Rocket will have everything the same like BWU but without the e2e CI
- Backwpup has the same workflow, but the e2e is only on local to test. 

I've added Backwpup pro to the workspace so you can check the `.aiassistant` from there as well.

## wporg-mcp-server
WordPress.org MCP Server — provides tools, resources, and prompts for interacting with WordPress.org services.

Use prompts/list to discover available workflows for specific tasks. Browse wporg://* resources for reference documentation.

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
